comments.author: @ChaseFreedomMusician
comments.text: I did a talk on Neuromorphic compute in June 2023 at KCDC and it has MUCH bigger implications than those that you talk about here. The main thing is speed of inference. Because neuromorphic compute uses spiking neural networks under the hood they can be fine tuned on the fly. This has huge implications on hardware like PALM-E type robots because you have a State Action State loop. This means in faster than humans can process a machines can make decisions alter the world around them and that altering drives new state. This is the fast path to AGI because it's no longer request response it's a control loop.

comments.author: @MrLargonaut
comments.text: Nice, it sounds like a drastically more feasible route than quantum computing.  Instead of each bit being a superstate, in the neurochip each bit is based on that capacitance.  So it's not an 'infinite' number of states like quantum, but there'll be plenty of numbers between 0 and 1 to use per bit thanks to whatever precision they'll be able to control and monitor the capacitance of each bit.

comments.author: @Urgelt
comments.text:
Abandoning binary transistors and moving to nonbinary is a very old idea. Note: it need not be analog to do this. It can be digital - just more values than on-off are allowed.

Neuromorphic designs are analog, however.

Nonbinary chips are basically at the 1960 stage of development, I think. Large, power-hungry, bulky, low compute power. They're at the proof of concept stage, and researchers are floating ideas about how to program at the machine level.

If not for the quite sudden acceleration of AI on binary silicon, I would suggest that practical, commercially-viable nonbinary chips are several decades away.

Now I am not so sure.
